_comment: Ledger of recurring prose habits (constructions, gestures, paragraph/scene closers), the language-level counterpart to motifs.json. Nightly sessions read this before drafting and add entries after. Status: 'develop' = use only in a new form; 'rest' = do not use until rested_until chapter; 'watch' = fine in moderation. Saturday review prunes and logs counts.

constructions.pattern: 'the way [clause]' used as a trailing simile
constructions.example: the way you feel an old break in the weather before you feel the ache of it
constructions.note: Zero again in ch. 16, a delirium chapter built almost entirely out of manner-clause comparisons (the stairs, the voices, the courteous man) that was drafted with several 'the way X' constructions and had every one of them rewritten to a plain 'as' clause or cut, same remedy as ch. 15. Demoting to rest as flagged last time — five of the last six chapters at zero or one. Leave this construction alone for a real stretch; the plain-'as' replacement is doing the work now. Ch. 17 (first Maria chapter, new POV) drafted with nine instances of this exact shape on a first pass and every one was rewritten to a plain 'as' clause before the chapter was finished — the rest period holds even under a brand-new narrating voice; don't let POV novelty be an excuse to re-open it early. Ch. 18's first pass produced two more ('the room filled up with newsprint the way it had filled...', 'filed under history... the way the Attrition had become...') and both were rewritten, one to 'exactly as', one restructured entirely. Two chapters from the rest lifting, the pull toward this shape is still there every time; keep rewriting it out rather than assuming the habit is gone. Ch. 19's first pass produced the heaviest pull yet — eight separate instances across all four sections ('opened it the way other people say grace', 'the bad arm held the way a man holds a tool he trusts', 'the way he'd have told me the kettle had boiled', and five more) plus a 'the same way' variant, every one caught and rewritten to a plain 'as' clause, a flat declarative, or a restructured sentence before the chapter was finished. Ch. 20 hit the official end of the rest period and still came in at zero — a first pass produced six instances this time ('nodded the way a man nods at nothing in particular', 'much as the mine was the valley', others), every one rewritten to a plain 'as' or 'much as' clause, or restructured into two sentences, before the chapter was finished. Extending the rest rather than lifting it: four chapters running now where a draft pass reaches for this shape repeatedly and the only thing holding the count at zero is deliberate rewriting, not the habit actually fading. Ch. 21's first pass produced five instances ('Lloyd woke the way he always wakes', 'the way a man says a thing he has only just decided', 'the way Edie gives a report', 'the way we took Vantry to it', 'the way he meant it'), every one rewritten to a plain 'as' clause, 'like', or a restructured sentence before the chapter was finished — the pull is, if anything, stronger under confrontation-heavy dialogue scenes than it was in quieter chapters. Don't lift the rest on the calendar again until a chapter's first pass comes in clean on its own.

constructions.example: a thing to explain; a thing your body has quietly decided
constructions.note: Seventh chapter running at zero, including ch. 16, where a vague placeholder noun would have been the easy way to gesture at everything delirium left unnamed and wasn't reached for even once. Safe to consider this one fully retired rather than merely resting. Eighth clean chapter now in ch. 17 — a first draft used 'a thing' twice (Maria's new voice reaching for the same vague filler) and both were replaced with 'something' or cut. Treat as fully retired across POVs, not just Lloyd's. Ninth clean chapter in ch. 18 — a first draft used it twice more ('not a thing she said', 'hiding a thing from me') and both were rephrased ('that sort of thing', 'anything'). Fully retired; stop flagging unless it reappears. It reappears in ch. 19, twice, but in a different shape worth distinguishing from the retired filler: 'what a thing was worth' and 'what the Church meant when it called a thing settled' both use 'a thing' as a specific, load-bearing noun echoing the chapter's own title, not a vague placeholder standing in for something unnamed. Left in deliberately rather than cut. Keep watching for the vague-filler version returning, but don't flag this title-echo usage as a lapse. Ch. 20 back to zero, no title-echo opportunity this time either — tenth clean chapter overall for the vague-filler form. Ch. 21's first draft used it twice ('a thing he's been caught at', 'a thing he has only just decided') and both were replaced with 'whatever' and 'something' before the chapter was finished — eleventh clean chapter in the final text.

constructions.pattern: 'I have learned/found/never...' followed by a general rule
constructions.example: I have learned the exact weight a thing has to reach before it's worth the cost of saying it out loud
constructions.note: Seventh chapter running at zero. A draft pass of ch. 16 produced a near-miss ('is, I have come to understand, a different skill altogether') in the Ivet beat and it was cut back to a plain statement with no self-aware hedge. Stays on watch rather than retired, since the delirium register makes this one easy to slip back into. Ch. 17 (Maria, new POV) stayed clean of the general-rule shape, but see the new 'i-have-anaphora' entry below — her confessional voice reaches for 'I have [verb]' sentence openers constantly, and this aphorism pattern is the thing that habit could calcify into if a later chapter lets one of those openers run on into a stated general rule instead of a flat personal fact. Ch. 18 stayed clean too, and went further than clean: the chapter drops 'I have' openers to zero entirely (see i-have-anaphora) rather than letting one calcify into this pattern, though a few present-tense generalizations slipped in elsewhere ('there is nothing left over to accuse') as flat institutional observation rather than self-aware personal rule — different enough in register to leave off this ledger, but worth a glance next time. Ch. 19 stays clean again, and the Edie ledger scene offered an obvious opening ('I have learned that a thing's worth and its cost are never the same question') that was written instead as two flat declaratives with no stated rule attached. Ch. 20 stays clean too, eleventh chapter running — the closest the chapter came was the valley-works explanation ('I had taken it for the kind of fact a person mentions once and sets down'), which stays a flat personal fact about one specific thing rather than a general rule about facts or people. Ch. 21 stays clean too, twelfth chapter running, despite a confession scene built almost entirely out of Lloyd stating flat personal reasons — none of them generalized into a rule about people or trust.

Ch. 16 at 19, same band held through a whole-chapter unreliable-narration experiment. Contrast partner rotated to its most minimal form yet: Lloyd's long, overlapping delirium sentences pulled up short by Maria's bare grounding words reaching him from outside the slide (cup. window. blanket. her own hand.) rather than by another character's combat calls or institutional paperwork. Ch. 17 (first Maria chapter) holds the same band at 22, and did rotate the contrast partner as flagged: her long, looping guilt-sentences get cut short by plain nursing fact ('I did that.' 'I have checked.') rather than by anyone's dialogue. Keep watching that the short side doesn't collapse into the new i-have-anaphora habit below instead of staying genuinely varied. Ch. 18 drops to 14 — a real dip, not noise — because the chapter leans on short declarative dialogue (Lloyd and Edie both terse by canon) and bureaucratic one-liners ('Nobody senior was charged.') as its contrast partner instead of another long sentence immediately following. Worth deciding whether 18-22 or occasional dips into the mid-teens is the real band for Maria's voice before flagging a trend either way. Ch. 19 climbs back to 21, closer to the 17/18 pre-dip high than the ch. 18 low, with a third contrast partner this time: Edie's ledger lines and one-word exchanges ('Good.' 'Work.' 'Said if.') cutting against Maria's looping sums. The 18-22 band looks like the real one; ch. 18's 14 reads as the outlier, tied to that chapter's unusually dialogue-light newsprint sections, rather than the start of a downward trend. Ch. 20 pushes past the band to 24, the highest yet — a quiet, connective chapter whose three expository movements (settling in, the accumulating pattern, the three discarded explanations) run long by nature, and the contrast partner this time is the clipped chop-house exchange with the Indemnity clerk ('Latch till noon,' 'bolted after,' 'Shut Tuesdays, carpet men in') plus the bare one-line reveal 'Halvard Crane.' Ch. 21 drops back to 16, below even the ch. 18 dip, because a confession scene built mostly out of two-line exchanges ('Yes.' 'You're going to kill him.' 'Yes.') leaves far less room for Maria's looping sentences to run long in the first place — the short side isn't a contrast partner cutting off a long sentence this time, it's most of the scene. 24 at ch. 20 now reads as the real outlier, tied to that chapter's explanation-heavy shape, same as ch. 18's 14 was; the 18-22 band holds for ordinary chapters and dips hard whenever the scene itself is mostly short confrontational dialogue.

constructions.pattern: 'same as [clause]' used as a trailing comparison, the direct replacement for the rested the-way-simile
constructions.example: same as I run all of them back now
constructions.note: Four chapters running at exactly one use (Maria's hand on his chest, 'the same as I had every single time since the chapel'). Settled, controlled background usage. Ch. 17 drops to zero — the first chapter not to reach for it at all — likely just the new POV finding its own shapes rather than a deliberate rest; worth checking whether it resumes at one in ch. 18 before reading anything into the dip. It resumed in ch. 18, at two rather than one ('same as she always did', 'same as I set down anything I can't carry') — both load-bearing rather than decorative, but worth holding at one going forward rather than letting it creep upward now that it's also absorbing some of the retired the-way-simile's old work. Ch. 19 held at exactly one as instructed ('same as he asked anything he already half expected would go unanswered', Lloyd asking what's in Carrowgate) — a second natural opening (the gaslamps, 'punctual regardless') was deliberately rewritten without the construction to keep the count down. The one-per-chapter discipline is holding. Ch. 20 held at exactly one again ('Lloyd walked every evening, same as he had in Vantry') — a second opening, in the three-discarded-reasons paragraph, was deliberately written as 'much as' instead to keep the count down. See the new 'as-if-comparison' entry below: that construction, not this one, absorbed most of this chapter's comparison load. Ch. 21 held at exactly one again ('he said it without heat, same as he says everything') — the discipline is five chapters deep now and looks like the real steady state for this construction rather than a rule still being actively enforced.

constructions.pattern: Lloyd narrates his own perception-management in filing/accounting/procedural language
constructions.example: filed and closed and not brought up again; I did the sum; running the frame back
constructions.note: Sixth chapter running clean. Ch. 16 was the strongest possible temptation for this one — a whole chapter of Lloyd trying to manage facts he can't otherwise process, including the knot-cord count — and it still reached for arithmetic as a dry joke rather than filing language. Treat as effectively retired. Ch. 16 was also Lloyd's last chapter on the page for the whole of Act III: the POV has moved to Maria for ch. 17-25, and since this construction is defined around Lloyd's specific filing-and-accounting self-talk, it's dormant rather than tracked for the Maria chapters — pick it back up only if the narration returns to Lloyd.

constructions.pattern: a clause restated through its own negation for flat understatement — 'didn't X because there wasn't X to do', 'wasn't an answer that wasn't Y'
constructions.example: she didn't say anything useful, because there wasn't anything useful to say; I didn't have an answer that wasn't the same thing said back to her, worse
constructions.note: Sixth chapter running without it. Not reached for in ch. 16 either, despite several places (the buried memory, the cord) where a negated restatement would have been an easy shape to default to; still safe to use if it arises naturally, not a default. Seventh clean chapter in ch. 17, carrying the habit's absence across the Act III POV change. Eighth clean chapter in ch. 18, including the letter scene, which had an obvious opening for it ('there wasn't a threat that wasn't...') and used a plainer construction instead ('There was no threat folded anywhere inside it'). Ninth clean chapter in ch. 19 — the farewell scene's 'not her fare, not a hand with the bag, not so much as a kind word' runs on repeated plain negation instead, a different and so far untracked anaphoric shape, not this one. Tenth clean chapter in ch. 20. Eleventh clean chapter in ch. 21, despite the confession's several obvious openings for it (what he didn't tell her, what the plan wasn't).

constructions.pattern: a statement capped with a trailing 'which was/is [flat judgment]' clause
constructions.example: which was true, and also the kindest thing she could have said to her just then; which was as much of a question as Edie generally asks
constructions.note: Four chapters clean now. A draft pass of ch. 16's opening produced one bare trailing 'which told me...' close and it was split into two short declaratives instead, same remedy as ch. 12-13. Treat any return to the bare trailing-'which' shape as a real lapse. Ch. 17's first draft produced two more (Edie's visit, the prayer paragraph) and both were split into separate declarative sentences before the chapter was finished, same remedy again — this is clearly the construction Maria's looping, qualifying sentences most want to fall into, so keep watching every chapter of hers for it, not just occasionally. Ch. 18's first draft produced five more (Lloyd's silence, the carrying metaphor, the landlady's tact, Edie leaving the letter, the library shelving), every one split into separate sentences before the chapter was finished — the highest single-draft count yet for this construction, in a chapter built almost entirely out of exactly the explanatory-aside material ('she did X, which meant Y') this pattern feeds on. Treat this as the construction most likely to reappear unedited in a rushed draft; it is being caught, not avoided by instinct. Ch. 19's first draft produced one more, in the ledger scene ('she had only ever cared what it cost, which I had slowly come to understand were not the same question at all, and that she was the only one... who had never once confused them') — split into three short declaratives before the chapter was finished. Still being caught every single chapter; five chapters running in a row now where a draft pass reaches for this shape at least once. Ch. 20's first draft produced two more (the Senate skyline, the Indemnity-pin realisation — 'which is exactly why it took me two weeks...') and both were split into separate sentences before the chapter was finished. Six chapters running where the final text stays clean. Ch. 21's first draft produced two more (the opening 'he woke at the usual hour, which was the first wrong thing...' and the quiet-answer beat, 'which would itself have told me something') and both were split into separate sentences before the chapter was finished — seven chapters running clean in the final text, still never clean on a first pass.

constructions.pattern: a short sentence opens with 'I have [verb]' as a flat, ledger-like confessional statement — a new habit, first seen in Maria's own first-person voice
constructions.example: I have checked. I have turned the arithmetic of that every way it will go. I have tried the sentence several ways and none of them let me off.
constructions.note: New in ch. 17, Maria's first chapter as narrator — five instances, all in the two interior reckoning paragraphs (the prayer, the Vail wound, the register). Distinct from the retired i-have-learned-aphorism: no general rule gets stated, each one is a flat personal fact standing on its own, closer to a confession she's logging than an observation about how the world works. Reads as earned characterisation right now — her guilt literalised as bookkeeping — but five in one chapter is enough to flag. Watch ch. 18-19 for whether it keeps recurring at this rate; if so, it wants evolving (vary the opener, or let a later chapter withhold it deliberately) rather than repeating as a default confessional tic. Ch. 18 drops it to zero outright — deliberately withheld, per the note above, since her attention this chapter is on the newspapers and the institution rather than her own private ledger. But see the i-had-anaphora entry below: the same confessional impulse resurfaced in the past-perfect instead of the present-perfect, which is evolution in tense only, not in kind. Don't credit ch. 18 with having retired the habit; it relocated. Ch. 19 holds at zero again, and this time i-had-anaphora also drops to zero — see below for the fronting technique that did it. Ch. 20 holds at zero too, a third clean chapter for the present-perfect variant specifically. Ch. 21 holds at zero again, a fourth clean chapter — fitting, since the chapter's confessional weight belongs to Lloyd this time, not Maria's own ledger-keeping.

constructions.pattern: a sentence opens with 'I had [verb]' as a flat retrospective anaphora — the past-perfect cousin of i-have-anaphora, used the chapter that habit was deliberately withheld
constructions.example: I had read Anse Duley's name in it most nights for six weeks. I had not decided, until Edie's hand was actually out for it, whether I could put it in that hand.
constructions.note: New in ch. 18. Seven instances, spread across all three sections rather than clustered in one reckoning paragraph the way i-have-anaphora was in ch. 17 — this version reads more like a structural habit of hers than a confined confessional outburst, which may make it harder to notice and easier to let calcify. Watch ch. 19-20 for whether Maria's narration keeps reaching for 'I had' as a default sentence opener regardless of which present-perfect or past-perfect variant is in use; if both keep recurring under different tenses, the real habit is the anaphoric 'I have/had [verb]' opener itself, and it may be worth merging these two entries and evolving the shape rather than tracking the tenses separately. Ch. 19's first draft had five sentence-initial 'I had [verb]' openers; every one was rewritten before the chapter was finished, mostly by moving an adverbial phrase ('Three days before,', 'Slowly,') to the front of the sentence so the clause lands mid-sentence instead of as the opener, keeping the underlying fact. Final count zero for both variants, confirming the real habit is the sentence-initial position itself rather than either tense. Ch. 20's first draft had three sentence-initial 'I had [verb]' openers ('I had lived with that habit...', 'I had seen him learn a man like that before...', 'I had never seen him spend three weeks...'); two were fixed by fronting an adverbial or relocating the clause mid-sentence, and the third ('I had taken it for the kind of fact...', the Crane-name recognition) was judged load-bearing enough as a flat personal fact to leave in rather than force out at the cost of a worse sentence — final count one, not zero, a deliberate exception rather than a miss. Ch. 21 held at exactly one again ('I had asked him, more than once, why a man so plainly fond of his mother had stayed away so long'), the same kind of load-bearing flat fact as the ch. 20 exception, left in rather than forced out. Two chapters running now at exactly one — this may be settling into a one-per-chapter allowance rather than a zero target. Recommend merging these two entries next review into one 'i-have/had-anaphora' entry tracking opener position across both tenses, and keep using the adverbial-fronting fix as the default, with an occasional single exception allowed when the plain opener is genuinely the clearest sentence.

constructions.pattern: 'as if [clause]' used as a trailing or embedded comparison — a new habit, first seen at volume in Maria's Act III voice
constructions.example: a splinter I meant to deal with and then mostly didn't; pressed flat as if it had lived under something heavy for most of its life
constructions.note: New in ch. 20 — three instances across the chapter (the splinter aside, the pressed-flat coat paper, the clerk's flat unhurried question), none clustered in one paragraph. Worth flagging early precisely because of what retired it last time: 'the way X' was put on an extended rest this chapter and 'same as' is being deliberately held to one per chapter, and this is the shape that's quietly absorbing the overflow. Not a problem yet at three, but watch ch. 21-23 for whether it climbs the way 'same as' once threatened to, and consider capping it the same way (one or two per chapter) before it calcifies rather than after. Ch. 21 drops it to zero — a confession scene built mostly out of flat dialogue and direct accounting gave it nowhere natural to land. One data point only; don't read a trend into a chapter shape (short, dialogue-heavy) that wasn't built to use comparisons much at all.

closers.pattern: paragraph or chapter ends on the narrator stating what he did not say, or what the scene means
closers.example: I said none of that. I hadn't said anything since the school wall and didn't start now.
closers.note: Ch. 15 and ch. 16 both avoid it. Ch. 16 ends on a bare image — daylight through the gap in the Callow Ford roof, mid-slide, no resolving line and nothing stated about what it means — which is the chapter's own outline requirement (no lucid interval, no final clarity) as much as it is this ledger's preference. Three chapters (12-14) still the longest run on this pattern; neither ch. 15 nor ch. 16 is added to the chapters list. Ch. 17 also avoids it: ends on Maria's hand on Lloyd's chest and the plain fact of feeling him believe her, not on any statement of what the moment meant. Four chapters clean running into Act III. Ch. 18 keeps the streak: ends on the letter folded away into the floorboard gap the register left, a plain action on a plain object, with no line stating what keeping-and-not-answering it means. Five chapters clean. Ch. 19 keeps it going: ends on Edie's footsteps fading down the stair and the paper still in Maria's hand, nothing stated about what the realisation (that Edie never once asked them for anything) means or costs — the realisation itself is shown as the outline's own beat, landed through what Edie didn't do, not through the narrator glossing it afterward. Six chapters clean. Ch. 20 extends it: ends on Maria standing with the floor plan open in both hands, unable to fold it back along its own creases because her hands won't hold steady — the shake stands in for the fear and the decision ahead of her, with no line naming either. Seven chapters clean. Ch. 21 extends it again: ends on Lloyd's own line of dialogue, 'Tell me I'm wrong about him. If I am. You'd know before I would,' with no narrator gloss on what his asking costs either of them. Eight chapters clean.

closers.pattern: chapter ends on an image of something indifferent or inanimate personified as 'patient', waiting out time without hurry
closers.example: the night came down slow over the burnt manse... patient, working at the dark the way it works at everything, given enough time and no one to tell it to stop
closers.note: Spent at ch. 08-09 review; stayed spent through ch. 13. Do not return to 'patient' as a chapter-ending word.
